articles.headline: Thousands March in London Supporting Palestinians
articles.dek: Demonstrators called for a UK ceasefire and an end to arms sales to Israel, with police making 20 arrests.
articles.lead: Thousands of people gathered in central London on Saturday to express support for Palestinians, calling for an end to what they described as genocide. The demonstration, which began on the Embankment, saw participants marching towards parliament with flags and placards.
articles.takeaway: Demonstrators called for a UK ceasefire and an end to arms sales to Israel, with police making 20 arrests.
body: Thousands of people gathered in central London on Saturday to express support for Palestinians, calling for an end to what they described as genocide. The demonstration, which began on the Embankment, saw participants marching towards parliament with flags and placards.

Organizers stated that 250,000 people attended the National March For Palestine. Protesters urged the UK government to cease supplying arms to Israel, citing reports from organizations including the UN and Amnesty International that allege genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. A minute of silence was observed for lives lost in Gaza.

The Metropolitan police reported 20 arrests were made during the event. These included charges for criminal damage after some individuals climbed onto the Battle of Britain memorial, as well as assaulting police officers. Some arrests were also made on suspicion of supporting a proscribed organization.

The march comes after the UK foreign secretary announced sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements and declared the UK government's position that the occupation of the West Bank is unlawful. He also stated that settlers, supported by the Israeli government, are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.

The Palestine Coalition, which organized the march, has held over 30 demonstrations since October 2023. A counter-protest by Stop The Hate also took place. Police imposed conditions on both events to minimize disruption, including designated routes and times for the main march and rally.

articles.dek: A joint operation by the Financial Conduct Authority and the National Crime Agency has led to three arrests in connection with a suspected insider dealing ring.
articles.lead: Three individuals have been arrested as part of a significant operation targeting a criminal insider dealing ring. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) and the National Crime Agency (NCA) collaborated on the investigation, which involved raids on five residential properties in London and Manchester.
articles.takeaway: A joint operation by the Financial Conduct Authority and the National Crime Agency has led to three arrests in connection with a suspected insider dealing ring.
body: Three individuals have been arrested as part of a significant operation targeting a criminal insider dealing ring. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) and the National Crime Agency (NCA) collaborated on the investigation, which involved raids on five residential properties in London and Manchester.

Over 100 staff from both agencies participated in the coordinated raids. During the operation, authorities seized more than 30 electronic devices, including phones, computers, and tablets. The suspects were taken for interviews following their arrests.

Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, emphasized the seriousness of insider dealing, stating it poses a significant threat to market integrity. He affirmed the commitment to using all available powers to combat serious and organised crime groups involved in market abuse.

Nikhil Rathi, chief executive of the FCA, described the operation as a major undertaking against suspected criminal activity. He noted the regulator's increasingly assertive actions, working with bodies like the Takeover Panel and financial institutions, to address potential inappropriate disclosure of information.

The FCA has previously identified abnormal share movements before takeover announcements, with concerns that some instances may involve the leaking of inside information. Rathi highlighted that organised criminal groups are increasingly sophisticated and view insider dealing as a profitable business model globally.

body: Poor e-bike parking has been an issue seen by all of London's councils Westminster City Council is issuing thousands more fines for badly parked dockless e-bikes since it began its enforcement crackdown on rogue parking.
So far more than 5,000 fixed penalty notices (FPN) have been given to operators since the start of the 2026-27 financial year, while only 1,259 were issued the previous year.
A sub-committee heard that if the crackdown continued at the same rate, Westminster was forecast to issue 9,648 dockless bike FPNs by the end of the year – a potential seven-fold increase.
E-bike rental firms Forest, Voi, Bolt and Lime have previously said they supported efforts to tackle poor parking and were working to encourage responsible use of their e-bikes.
Enforcement is mostly focused around 20 hotspots for irresponsible dockless e-bike parking, many of which are in the West End and St James's wards, a Westminster City Council sub-committee heard.

Cabinet member for enforcement, Caroline Sargent, said: "Sometimes hundreds of bikes are really seriously blocking the road, going into the road. So that is where the main seizure action is taking place, but the enforcement action is taking place in every ward.

Last month, developers submitted plans for the site’s 16 remaining acres. Chee Sing Siew, the Battersea Power Station Development Company’s finance chief, told City AM the project “depends on patient capital and a shared belief in the long-term value a place can create”.He added: “Against a quieter property market, the continued support from our lenders reflects confidence in the transformation achieved so far, from the restoration of the once derelict Grade II-star listed Power Station to the creation of a thriving riverside neighbourhood, and the opportunity that lies ahead.“[The refinancing] provides a firm financial foundation for developing the remaining 16 acres of land and creates sustained value for our shareholders and the wider neighbourhood.”Elton John opened new venueConstruction on the development’s latest addition, Prospect Place South, is set to begin in September.

The two buildings included in this phase will deliver about 300 new homes and 65,000 sq ft of retail, hospitality and leisure space.Battersea Power Station is already home to more than 2,200 homes, about 800,000 sq ft of office space and more than 170 shops, bars and restaurants.

A consortium of Malaysian investors bought the site in 2012 with plans to redevelop it for £400m. Since they stepped in to take the project out of administration, these shareholders have invested more than £5bn in its redevelopment.The redeveloped Battersea Power Station already hosts businesses including Apple, appliance maker SharkNinja and architectural firm Foster + Partners.

The original Battersea Power Station was designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott, an art deco architect famed for London’s red telephone boxes and the Bankside Power Station, which now hosts the Tate Modern art gallery.

The site operated as a coal-fired power station until it was decommissioned in 1975.The building is now home to Apple Music Hall, a live music venue which hosted Sir Elton John for its first concert last month.

body: Monday 12 October 2026 12:25 pm | Updated: Monday 12 October 2026 1:17 pm The Bank of England has been targeted in an inflation installation stunt in the centre of the City of London.Over the weekend, a satirical art piece appeared across the road from the central bank’s office on Threadneedle Street.A black Canon printer, sitting atop a decorative silver-beaded pedestal surrounded by a stream of banknotes, was locked inside a tall transparent display case.

The case, held up by a bright red frame, reads: “In case of emergency inflation. Break Glass.”A pair of black handcuffs was also resting on the base of the pedestal.The installation appears to satirise a Bank of England strategy known as “quantitative easing,” that involves the creation of new money to purchase government bonds from private institutions.The method aims to inject liquidity into the financial system in a bid to lower interest rates, encourage borrowing and stimulate spending.

The Bank first started the programme in March 2009 following the financial crisis. In 2022, it began to reverse the operation with quantitative tightening, where it allowed bonds to mature without replacing them.

Last month, the Bank laid out plans to slow down its reduction pace to ease pressure on public debt markets and bond yields.Mystery artist plays on inflation fearsQuestions are swirling in the City over who was behind the installation, with the style matching previous works of political street artist Banksy.

Earlier this year it emerged that the removal of three Banksy stunts in London had cost taxpayers nearly £150,000.The largest of those bills related to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in London in September 2025, which came with a hefty removal price tag of £85,000.
A spokesperson for Banksy confirmed they were not behind the Bank stunt.The new stunt targeting the Bank comes as inflation fears in the UK rise following economic turmoil from the Iran war.

We’ve been steadily building momentum in the UK over the last few years (via regular flights on Norwegian Air) but now I had San Francisco as a potential option.

body: Mark Rowley says inclusivity is crucial for the force and he refuses to be ‘blown off course’ by critics Sir Mark Rowley: I will have more police officers of colour in the UK capital – and the culture wars won’t stop me doing it Mark Rowley has said the Metropolitan police must recruit more black and Asian officers in order to gain the trust of minority ethnic communities in London, and vowed not to be “blown off course by the culture wars”.

The right has criticised drives for diversity, claiming they lead to lower standards. Rowley, who is commissioner of the Met and Britain’s top police officer, said that as a leader of a major organisation he was prepared to take a stand against the “toxicity” surrounding the diversity debate and criticised other leaders for “running away from the subject”.

In London, 46% of people are from a minority ethnic background, compared with 18% of Met officers. Rowley said he was driven by operational necessity, not politics, and believed “inclusivity” was vital to policing by consent, which is the philosophical cornerstone of British policing.

“We cannot police London effectively if we fail to recruit from all of London,” he writes in the Guardian. “Effective policing depends upon inclusivity. If you are committed to policing by consent which stands or falls on the trust of all communities, you cannot do without it.” He writes: “Today, we are launching a major recruitment campaign.

We have no interest in the politics and ideologies of the culture wars. Inclusion is an operational necessity. “We cannot be effective if large sections of society do not trust us, do not work with us or do not see policing as a service that understands their experiences.

An inclusive workforce is not a public relations exercise. It makes us better at protecting victims, catching criminals and preventing crime.” Rowley is braced for attacks from some on the left who may say his force is not going far enough, as well as from those on the right who are critical of diversity, equity and inclusivity (DEI) initiatives.

The document warns that the dearth of new listings in London is a “strategic growth problem” which poses a challenge to the UK economy as a whole, not just the stock exchange.“The UK is at a serious risk of becoming forever an incubator nation, exporting its greatest companies just at the point they become globally consequential,” the document, reported by the Sunday Times, is understood to say.Cmit has handed a set of demands to the Chancellor which it says would encourage a glut of new listings and more prevent promising start-ups from being lost to other countries like the US.The City chiefs acknowledged that Healey is unlikely to abolish stamp duty on shares because it raises £3bn for government coffers every year.

But the levy could be removed for pension funds and individual savings accounts (ISAs), the group said.IPO drought ‘problem for Britain’Cmit said the Treasury should consider an inheritance tax relief on pensions invested in the UK over a 15-year period, though it sought to sidestep fears that pensions would be forced to invest in UK shares.The government could mobilise as much as £125bn in equity by 2042 by introducing a 10 per cent tax credit on dividends required by pension funds, at an annual cost to the Treasury of up to £742m.Cmit pointed to the £24bn sale of Cambridge-based Arm Holdings to Japanese conglomerate SoftBank as an example of the “shrinking” of London’s IPO pipeline.Mark Austin, a capital markets lawyer and a member of Cmit, told the Sunday Times the group’s ideas would “mobilise long-term domestic capital into UK companies, while respecting a fiscally constrained environment and keeping cost capped, design choices voluntary and fiduciary duties intact”.A suite of London-listed firms have quit the UK’s public markets this year, with the value of bids for listed companies totalling at least £70bn.

Insurance firm Beazley, asset manager Schroders and property giant Segro are among those to have accepted takeovers.Andrea Rossi, chief executive of FTSE 100 finance firm M&G, wrote in the Sunday Times this weekend that the “decline of London’s stock market” is a “problem for Britain”.Alongside the exit of listed firms and promising start-ups, City chiefs have bemoaned a lack of big-ticket IPOs in London.
Earlier this week, hopes of a £7bn float for high street giant Boots were scuppered by its sale to the billionaire Weston family.

body: Friday 09 October 2026 12:25 pm | Updated: Friday 09 October 2026 12:36 pm Rent: musical now plays at the Tom Stoppard Theatre Rent musical review and star rating: ★★★It’s pertinently ironic that Rent’s press night coincided with the London Film Festival premiere of Elsinore, Andrew Scott’s remarkably tender AIDS drama.

Perhaps in the late-eighties when this musical was conceived, even talking about the epidemic on a stage was politically powerful, even if it were sprinkled as a theme rather than addressed head-on like dramas do today.

By those standards, Jonathan Larson’s Rent, which follows a group of creatives fighting eviction from their New York building, was once fearsomely progressive. But by today’s standards, taking something so horrific as AIDS, which took the lives of 20,000 Brits alone, and putting it as a backdrop to a central story about people getting kicked out of their flats (which is dealt with with far more emotion) feels strange and tone deaf.Rent musical: go for the musicIn act 2 there is one attempt to go beyond two-dimensional representation with the platforming of the death of one character, Angel, to the disease, which is treated with more sensitivity via the track I’ll Cover You, but this production lets down the attempt: dressed in y-fronts and disappearing within sheets, Angel’s death feels bizarre and emotionless rather than profound.

Regardless, the pop-rock songs are fun, most notably Seasons of Love, famous more recently from Glee, even if many are strangely buoyant given they’re often about dying and how many of the characters have the disease.

If Rent is for one thing, it is taking in these spectacular songbooks, which includes bangers like La Vie Bohème, One Song Glory and Take Me Or Leave Me. Olivier Award-winner Luke Sheppard’s conventional production doesn’t play much with the formula; David Woodhead’s set is similarly predictable, centring upon a shabby-looking apartment.Huge fan cloutBeyond that though, the story line often there to service the arrival of the next song rather than advancing the plot, especially when central character Mimi is about to die from AIDS related conditions but is saved when her partner Doug walks in and apparently sings her back to life, which feels problematic in just about every way possible.Anyway, who cares what I think, Rent holds huge fan clout.
Sit back and listen to the music and you’ll have a nice time. Rent plays at The Tom Stoppard Theatre until 29 May 2027

In February, Vincent Chan was jailed after pleading guilty to 56 offences, including assault by penetration on three-year-old girls in his care at a Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road in north-west London.

Bright Horizons referred the matter to Camden council, which advised the nursery to investigate. Chan was put on duties that involved no contact with children while the investigation by Bright Horizons took place.

After it was completed, Chan was cleared to return to his role caring for young children in the nursery. A year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself sexually abusing three-year-old girls at the Bright Horizons nursery.

body: Lewisham Council in southeast London is developing a new housing strategy that includes transferring public land to community groups for the construction of social housing. Under the plan, packages of public land valued up to £2 million each could be given to organizations like housing co-operatives, with the condition that they build social housing.

The council is also considering placing any land transferred through this program into community land trusts to ensure permanent affordability. To further support these initiatives, low-interest loans and pre-approved planning permission may be offered to expedite construction. These proposals are expected to be implemented within a year.

This approach aims to address the UK's housing crisis by empowering community-led organizations to build essential housing, a model less common in the UK compared to European economies. Currently, most new homes are built by for-profit developers, who often negotiate down the amount of social housing included in larger developments.

Daniel Dream, Lewisham's cabinet member for inclusive regeneration, planning and housing delivery, stated that the current system of negotiating with private developers is insufficient for meeting social housing needs. He believes empowering community organizations through public land is a more effective strategy.

The strategy leverages a loophole in a 1972 law, which obliges public bodies to accept the highest offer for land. However, for sites valued at £2 million or less, councils can choose the buyer and sale price, even giving the land away for free, if it offers positive benefits to the area.

This initiative could be particularly effective in utilizing small, underused sites, which are often overlooked by major developers. Lewisham has identified potential for up to 9,700 new homes on over 3,000 small sites, contributing to higher quality housing and neighborhood improvements.

body: Friday 09 October 2026 3:24 pm Banks are bracing for a potential Budget tax raid. Top finance industry chiefs have warned the Chancellor that hiking taxes on the banking sector in the forthcoming Budget could drive businesses and capital out of the UK.Bosses of the City’s biggest industry bodies – including UK Finance, TheCityUK and the CBI – have written to John Healey calling for him to avoid raising the tax rate on banks.

“Tax decisions should be assessed not simply by the revenue they are expected to raise in the short-term, but by their effects on investment, competitiveness and the capacity of firms to support households and businesses,” the group of City grandees said.

Healey met the top bosses of Britain’s biggest banks this week as speculation ramps up the industry will be used for a quick cash raid as Healey looks to rebuild his fiscal headroom that has been shattered by the Iran war.Economists have forecast that the £23.6bn in headroom left by former Rachel Reeves in the Spring Statement could have been slashed in half as a result of higher borrowing costs following the US-Iran war.Meanwhile, a number of top banks have upgraded their income forecast for the year on the expectation interest rates will remain higher for longer.The bosses warned Healey that banks already face an outsized tax rate when compared with competitors overseas.

Figures from PwC show total taxes on UK banks amount to 46 per cent of profits, compared to 42 percent in Amsterdam, 39 per cent in Frankfurt, 29 per cent in Dublin and 28 per cent in Dublin.Give banks same certainty other sectors get, say City chiefsBanks in the UK are subject to a sector-specific surcharge of three per cent that sits on top of corporation tax.
Some have suggested the surcharge could be returned to eight per cent as a way to raise revenue from banks, but other lobbyists have called for Healey to go further with a windfall tax.

The cohort of City bosses warned “a higher tax burden may not necessarily generate higher tax receipts if capital, people and businesses move elsewhere”.Signatories include TheCityUK boss Miles Celic, City Of London Corporation’s Chris Hayward, UK Finance’s David Postings, the CBI’s Rain Newton-Smith and AFME’s Adam Farkas.

body: More than 1,000 school support staff in south London are set to strike on Friday in a dispute over pay rates. Members of the GMB union, representing workers from over 30 schools in Merton and Greenwich, will participate in the industrial action.

The dispute centers on 'London weighting,' a supplement paid to staff in the capital. Support staff in these boroughs are currently paid at outer London rates, while teachers in the same schools receive inner London pay. The GMB union states that its members feel undervalued and are experiencing hardship due to this disparity.

Before the strike, union members are expected to rally outside Parliament, followed by a march to the Department for Education and on to Trafalgar Square. The GMB has requested a meeting with Education Secretary Lucy Powell to discuss the issue directly, but has not yet received a response.

Local councils acknowledge the concerns but state that the pay disparity can only be resolved at a national level. Merton Council explained that while they support fair pay, they cannot legally fund the increase locally. They also noted that the union's request for a one-off payment was not endorsed due to potential negative consequences for other council services.

A Greenwich Council spokesperson highlighted that the pay disparity dates back to 1990 when the Inner London Education Authority was abolished, and teachers retained inner London pay while support staff did not. Both councils indicated they are working with the government and other London boroughs to seek a national solution through a new negotiating body.

While borrowing costs and stretched affordability weigh on everyday buyers, the city’s richest residents are also making deep cuts to the prices of their multimillion-pound homes.This market is a world away from the rest of the UK property market – where the average house price was just under £275,000 in September, according to Nationwide.
